exam.subject: Agriculture
exam.title: ESSCE 2018 – Agriculture

parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions; each carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains six questions (20 points). Write your answers on the separate answer sheet.

source.note: Scanned paper; OCR text checked against the page images (options missing from the OCR were read from the images). The number printed on every page is 12.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Agriculture textbooks Grades 11 and 12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: A catch crop or an emergency crop is

options.A: quick growing annual grown when other crops have failed to produce grain.
options.B: grown in association with other crops.
options.C: cut and fed green for livestock.
options.D: planted to attract or trap insects.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Catch crops or emergence crops are quick-growing annuals that are sown in the field where crops have failed to produce grain', e.g. short-season millet.
B describes companion crops, C soiling crops and D trap crops. Answer: A.
tips: Soiling crop = cut and fed green; trap crop = attracts pests away from the main crop; green manure = ploughed in green.

similar_questions.stem: Crops that are cut and fed green to livestock, such as faba bean and field pea, are called
explanation_steps: The textbook calls crops cut and fed green to livestock 'soiling crops'.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of crops are horticultural crops?

options.A: Faba bean, field pea and wheat

explanation_steps: Horticultural crops are fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices and aromatic plants; cereals and pulses are field (agronomic) crops.
Cabbage and tomato are vegetables and orange is a fruit – all horticultural. The other groups contain cereals (wheat, barley, sorghum) or pulses (faba bean, field pea, chickpea, beans). Answer: D.
tips: Field crops = cereals, pulses, oil, fibre, forage crops grown on large areas; horticulture = fruits (pomology), vegetables (olericulture), flowers (floriculture).

similar_questions.stem: Which group consists only of field crops?
explanation_steps: Wheat (cereal), lentil (pulse) and sesame (oil crop) are field crops.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: Biological control in pest management involves the use of
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Biological control involves the use of natural enemies such as predators and diseases for the control of pests.'
Breeding/resistant varieties is a separate method; pesticides are chemical control. Answer: C.
tips: The same item appears as review question 2 at the end of G11 Unit 3.

similar_questions.stem: Releasing ladybird beetles to eat aphids in a field is an example of
explanation_steps: Ladybirds are natural enemies (predators) of aphids.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases – methods of pest control

questions.stem: Which of the following crops have long storage life?
explanation_steps: The G11 textbook's review question on storage gives 'wheat, barley and taff' as the crops with long storage life (the other choices there are oil seeds such as rapeseed and soybean).
Oil seeds (sesame, cotton seed) store poorly because of their high oil content. Wheat and taff is the textbook pair. Answer: C.
tips: Low moisture content, cool dry store and sound, undamaged seed lengthen storage life.

similar_questions.stem: Which factor shortens the storage life of seeds?
explanation_steps: Textbook: high relative humidity and temperature shorten the storage life of seeds.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.9 Threshing and Storage of Field Crops; Review question 3

questions.review_flag: The textbook supports 'wheat, barley and taff' (review question); sorghum and pearl millet (D) also store well in practice. Keyed C following the textbook.

questions.stem: Which of the following crops is not a member of cereals?
explanation_steps: Cereals are grasses grown for their edible, starchy grain: wheat, finger millet, sorghum, barley, taff, maize.
Lentil is a pulse (grain legume). Answer: C.
tips: Pulses: lentil, chickpea, faba bean, field pea, beans – rich in protein.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop is a pulse?
explanation_steps: Chickpea is a grain legume (pulse); the others are cereals.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following is different from the rest.
explanation_steps: Beans, sesame, groundnut and linseed are all annual FIELD crops (a pulse and oil crops).
Banana is a perennial horticultural (fruit) crop – the odd one out. Answer: A.
tips: Odd-one-out items: classify by use (cereal, pulse, oil, fruit), by life span or by field vs horticultural crop.

similar_questions.stem: Which one is different from the rest?
explanation_steps: Sorghum, barley, wheat and maize are cereals (field crops); orange is a fruit (horticultural).
Answer: D.

questions.review_flag: Poorly constructed: sesame, groundnut and linseed are oil crops, so both banana (fruit) and beans (pulse) differ from them. Keyed A (banana – the only horticultural, perennial crop).

questions.stem: According to the statistical data of the Ministry of Agriculture of 1997, the forest cover in Eritrea is estimated to be
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.2 (forest cover of Eritrea): 1912 – 30 %, 1952 – 11 %, 1960 – 5 %, 1997 – 1 %.
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, what was the forest cover of Eritrea in 1952?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following soil horizons consists of unconsolidated organic material, unsaturated with water?
explanation_steps: The O horizon is the surface layer of loose (unconsolidated) organic litter.
A = mineral topsoil with humus; B = subsoil (accumulation); C = weathered parent material; R = bedrock. Answer: D.
tips: Profile order from the top: O – A – B – C – R.

similar_questions.stem: The soil horizon made of unweathered bedrock is the
explanation_steps: R = rock (bedrock).
Answer: E.

questions.stem: A soil is acidic if the pH value is
explanation_steps: pH 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline.
Answer: E.
tips: 'Less than OR EQUAL to 7' wrongly includes neutral soil.

similar_questions.stem: A soil with pH 8.5 is
explanation_steps: pH > 7 means alkaline.
Answer: D.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – soil reaction

questions.stem: Which of the following meteorological instruments is used to measure the wind speed?
explanation_steps: An anemometer measures wind speed; a wind vane shows wind DIRECTION.
Barograph – air pressure; thermohygrograph – temperature and humidity; rain gauge – rainfall. Answer: B.
tips: Speed → anemometer; direction → wind vane.

similar_questions.stem: Which instrument records atmospheric pressure continuously?
explanation_steps: A barograph is a recording barometer.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an alternative source of energy?
explanation_steps: The textbook (2.4.3 Alternative Energy Sources) presents wind, solar and geothermal energy as renewable alternatives, and adds that 'kerosene and LPG are used to reduce the demand for wood' – i.e. kerosene is treated as an alternative to fuel wood.
In that textbook sense all four are alternatives to firewood. Answer: E.
Note: in general science kerosene is a fossil fuel, not a renewable alternative – see the review flag.
tips: In the Eritrean textbook 'alternative energy' means alternatives to fuel wood (to protect forests).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a renewable alternative energy source?
explanation_steps: Wind is renewable; the others are fossil fuels or wood-based.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Solar, geothermal and wind (A, C, D) are each correct on their own; kerosene is a fossil fuel. Keyed E because the textbook lists kerosene/LPG as alternatives to fuel wood. Teacher decision: E (textbook) – consider accepting A, C or D.

questions.stem: One of the following is not an advantage of bare-root seedlings.

options.A: Less complicated to grow in a nursery
options.C: Well suited to large nurseries for economical seed production
options.D: Roots are not exposed to air-drying during lifting, transplanting and planting

explanation_steps: Textbook advantages of bare-root seedlings: less complicated to grow, lighter to transport, suited to mechanisation and to large centralized nurseries, cheaper to produce.
Bare roots ARE exposed to drying during lifting and planting – protection of the roots is an advantage of containerized seedlings. Answer: D.
tips: Containerized = protected roots, longer planting period, but heavy and costly; bare-root = cheap and light, but roots can dry out.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of containerized seedlings over bare-root seedlings?

options.C: A longer planting period is possible

explanation_steps: Textbook: containerized seedlings allow a longer planting period; the other options are bare-root advantages.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.6 Seedling Planting – a) containerized and b) bare-root seedlings

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a physical soil and water conservation measure?
explanation_steps: Physical (mechanical) measures are structures or earthworks: terraces, bunds, land levelling, diversion ditches, check dams.
Crop rotation is an agronomic practice. Answer: C.
tips: Physical = structures; biological = vegetation; agronomic = how crops are grown.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is a biological soil and water conservation measure?
explanation_steps: Grass strips use vegetation.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Option B is printed 'Banding' – a misprint for 'Bunding' (bunds). No effect on the answer.

questions.stem: Dams are constructed for the purpose of water storage to be used for
explanation_steps: Dams store water for irrigation, power generation, domestic use and livestock watering (and flood control, fish).
Answer: E.
tips: Water-harvesting structures in the textbook: dams, ponds, river diversion, wells, roof and rock-outcrop harvesting.

similar_questions.stem: A small earthen reservoir dug to collect runoff for livestock and small irrigation is a
explanation_steps: Ponds store runoff water.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: When water accumulates in narrow channels during or immediately after heavy rains, it causes
explanation_steps: Rill erosion: runoff concentrates in many small, narrow channels (rills) during or just after heavy rain; rills can be removed by tillage.
Gullies are larger channels that tillage cannot remove. Answer: C.
tips: Sequence: splash → sheet → rill → gully.

similar_questions.stem: Removal of a thin, fairly uniform layer of soil by overland flow is
explanation_steps: Uniform thin-layer removal = sheet erosion.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: The two local breeds of cattle found in Eritrea are
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The breeds of cattle present in Eritrea are Barka, Arado and Arebo (Aden).' Holstein-Friesian is an introduced exotic breed.
Hassani is a goat breed and Shimejana a sheep breed. 'Arho' in option B is evidently 'Arebo', so B (Arado and Arebo) is the pair of local cattle breeds. Answer: B.
tips: Local cattle: Barka, Arado, Arebo (Aden); Dewhin on the Sudan border. Goats: Hassani, Barka (Tsa'adi). Sheep: Shimejana (Akele Guzai), Rashaidi.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a local goat breed of Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: goat breeds include the Hassani (Shukria).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3 Biodiversity – breeds of cattle in Eritrea

questions.review_flag: Option B reads 'Arado and Arho'; the textbook breed is 'Arebo (Aden)' – probable misprint. B is the only option with two local cattle breeds (A contains the exotic Holstein, C a goat breed).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an internal parasite?
explanation_steps: Lice, fleas, mites and ticks live on the skin or hair – they are all EXTERNAL parasites.
Internal parasites are worms (roundworms, tapeworms, liver flukes) and protozoa. Answer: E.
tips: External = on the body surface; internal = inside organs (gut, liver, lungs, blood).

similar_questions.stem: Which is an internal parasite of livestock?
explanation_steps: The liver fluke lives in the liver.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following animals have mono-gastric digestive system?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Pigs have a monogastric digestive system that is similar to that of humans. Poultry are also monogastric.'
Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants (four-compartment stomach).
So both C (pigs) and E (chicken) are correct; C is keyed, E is also accepted.
tips: Ruminants: cattle, sheep, goats (and camels as pseudo-ruminants). Monogastric: pigs, poultry, humans.

similar_questions.stem: Which animal is a ruminant?
explanation_steps: Goats have a rumen (four-compartment stomach).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.4 Types and Classification of Livestock – digestive systems

questions.review_flag: Two correct options: pigs (C) and chicken (E) are both monogastric according to the textbook. Both accepted; teacher decision on the official key.

questions.stem: The method of identification or marking, which reduces the value of hides and skins in livestock, is
explanation_steps: Branding burns numbers or designs into the skin with a hot iron or chemicals (textbook). The permanent scar damages the hide/skin and lowers its value.
Ear marks, ear notches and neck straps do not damage the body hide. Answer: A.
tips: Identification methods: tattooing, tagging, ear-notching, branding, neck straps.

similar_questions.stem: Which identification method uses a hot iron or chemicals on the skin?
explanation_steps: Textbook definition of branding.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Routine Management Practices – j) Methods used to identify livestock

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: the book describes branding but does not state that it lowers hide value; the answer follows standard animal-husbandry knowledge.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a working capital.
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Investment capital is essential for the purchase of irrigation systems, building materials, tractors, etc. Working capital is required for the day-to-day operation of the farm.'
Fertilizer is used up in one season – working capital. Tractor, irrigation canal, building and equipment are all long-term investment (fixed) capital.
So B, C, D and E are all 'not working capital'. D (building) is keyed; B, C and E are also accepted.
tips: Working (operating) capital: seed, fertilizer, fuel, feed, wages. Investment/fixed capital: land improvements, buildings, irrigation works, machinery.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of working capital on a farm?
explanation_steps: Seed and fertilizer are consumed in the production season – working capital.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Defective item: by the textbook's definition only fertilizer (A) is working capital, so B, C, D and E are all correct answers to 'not a working capital'. The setter probably meant 'Which is a working capital?' (answer A). Keyed D, accepting B–E. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: A budget used for small change in a farm plan is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'When a farmer proposes to introduce minor changes to a farm then a PARTIAL budget can be used to predict the expected change in profits.' A complete budget covers the whole farm.
'Partial budget' is not offered; 'minor budget' (B) is the option describing a budget for minor changes. Answer: B.
tips: Partial budget = only the costs and returns that change; complete budget = whole-farm plan.

similar_questions.stem: A budget that considers only the costs and returns affected by a proposed change is a
explanation_steps: Only changed items are included in a partial budget.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 4.2 Farm budgeting – partial and complete budget

questions.review_flag: The textbook term is 'partial budget', which is not among the options; 'minor budget' (B) is keyed as the intended answer ('E. None of the above' is arguable).

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the relationship between inputs and outputs?
explanation_steps: A production function states how the quantity of output depends on the quantities of inputs used, Y = f(X₁, X₂, …).
Answer: D.
tips: From the production function come total product, average product (AP = TP/X) and marginal product (MP = ΔTP/ΔX).

similar_questions.stem: Output per unit of variable input is called
explanation_steps: AP = TP ÷ quantity of input.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A farming system that allows the growing of perennial trees with annual crops is known as
explanation_steps: Agroforestry deliberately combines woody perennials (trees, shrubs) with annual crops and/or livestock on the same land.
Answer: C.
tips: Alley cropping is one agroforestry practice: crops grown between rows of trees/shrubs.

similar_questions.stem: Planting rows of leguminous shrubs with maize grown between the rows is
explanation_steps: Trees + crops in alleys = alley cropping, a form of agroforestry.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are advantages of wind power as an alternative energy source except that

options.B: it is a renewable source of energy.
options.C: farming and grazing is still possible on land occupied by wind turbines.
options.E: farms using wind power can be built off shore.

explanation_steps: The textbook lists A, B, C and E as advantages of wind power.
'Wind power is intermittent – constant wind is needed for uninterrupted supply' is listed as a DISADVANTAGE. Answer: D.
tips: Other disadvantage: large wind farms spoil the visual landscape.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of solar power according to the textbook?

options.B: It releases no water or air pollution

explanation_steps: Solar power generation releases no water or air pollution.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.4.3 Alternative Energy Sources – a) Wind power

questions.stem: Which of the following areas has the greatest density of livestock and major land degradation in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The Highlands of Eritrea are the areas of greatest livestock density and the areas of major land degradation.'
Answer: B.
tips: Water (sheet-and-rill) erosion is the most damaging form of land-resource loss in Eritrea; mean soil loss ≈ 42 t/ha/year.

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, the most damaging form of land-resource loss in Eritrea is
explanation_steps: The textbook names water (sheet-and-rill) erosion.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of chemical soil degradation?
explanation_steps: Textbook chemical degradation: loss of nutrients and organic matter, fixation of nutrients under alkaline conditions, salinization, acidification.
Deterioration of soil structure (compaction, crusting) is PHYSICAL degradation. Answer: C.
tips: Physical = structure, compaction, erosion; chemical = nutrients, salts, pH; biological = soil organisms and organic matter.

similar_questions.stem: Soil compaction by heavy machinery is an example of
explanation_steps: Compaction damages structure – physical.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a consequence of wild life decline in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: The decline of wildlife causes loss of biodiversity, economic losses (tourism, products) and ecosystem INSTABILITY.
Ecosystem stability is the opposite of a consequence of decline. Answer: D.
tips: Look for the option that contradicts the others.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a cause (not a consequence) of wildlife decline?
explanation_steps: Habitat destruction causes the decline.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All transactions of a farm are kept in an account book called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'All transactions of the farm must be kept in an accounts book called a journal. The journal records all receipts and expenses … chronologically.'
Answer: B.
tips: Petty cash book = small cash payments; wage book = labour and wages.

similar_questions.stem: Details of labour employed and wages paid are recorded in the
explanation_steps: Textbook: wages paid are recorded in the wage book.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A financial statement which reflects the financial position of a farm business on a specific date is called
explanation_steps: A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and net worth (owner's equity) at a specific date.
Answer: D.
tips: Balance sheet = position at a DATE; income statement = performance over a PERIOD.

similar_questions.stem: On a balance sheet, net worth equals
explanation_steps: Net worth = total assets − total liabilities.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are major distinguishing characteristics of cooperatives except that they have/are

options.C: run for the benefit of their members.

explanation_steps: Co-operatives are voluntary organisations owned and democratically controlled by their members, with an economic purpose, run for the members' benefit.
They are not owned by the State. Answer: D.
tips: Co-operative principles: voluntary open membership, democratic member control (one member one vote), member economic participation, autonomy.

similar_questions.stem: In a co-operative, decisions are usually made on the principle of
explanation_steps: Democratic control: one member, one vote.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Total revenue minus total cost is defined as
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'TC is required for computing net revenue (total revenue less TC).'
Net revenue is the same quantity as profit (when positive). C is the textbook term; A is also accepted.
tips: Net revenue > 0 → profit; < 0 → loss.

similar_questions.stem: A farm has total revenue 60,000 Nakfa, fixed cost 15,000 and variable cost 30,000 Nakfa. Its net revenue is
explanation_steps: Net revenue = 60,000 − 45,000 = 15,000 Nakfa. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: 'net revenue' (C, the textbook's term) and 'profit' (A) both mean total revenue − total cost. Both accepted.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about Eritrean agriculture?

options.A: Eritrea has remained at subsistence level for generations.
options.B: About 95% of cultivated land is managed by farmers and agro-pastoralists.
options.C: The main objective of subsistence farmers is to earn income from sale of products.
options.D: A small number of farmers concentrate on commercial production using modern technology.

explanation_steps: Subsistence farmers produce mainly to feed their own families, not to earn income from sales.
A, B and D describe Eritrean agriculture as presented in G11 Unit 1. Answer: C.
tips: Subsistence = production for home consumption; commercial = production for the market.

similar_questions.stem: The main aim of a commercial farmer is to
explanation_steps: Commercial farming is market-oriented.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The seasonal migration of people and livestock from hot lowlands to cool highlands during the hot season is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'the seasonal migration of people and livestock from hot lowlands to the cool highlands during the hot season is called transhumance.'
Answer: E.
tips: Transhumance is a form of semi-nomadic pastoralism (e.g. Sheeb area, Northern Red Sea).

similar_questions.stem: Farmers who live permanently in villages and keep both crops and livestock practise
explanation_steps: Settled crop + livestock farming = sedentary agro-pastoralism.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The branch of agriculture that deals with the production and handling of fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices & aromatic plants is known as
explanation_steps: Horticulture covers fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices and aromatic/medicinal plants.
Agronomy deals with field crops and soil management. Answer: A.
tips: Pomology (fruits), olericulture (vegetables), floriculture (flowers) are branches of horticulture.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of horticulture dealing with vegetables is
explanation_steps: Olericulture = vegetable growing.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Grasses grown for their edible seeds that are rich in carbohydrate are called
explanation_steps: Cereals are members of the grass family grown for their starchy (carbohydrate-rich) grain: wheat, barley, sorghum, maize, taff, millets.
Answer: C.
tips: Pulses are legumes rich in protein; oil crops are rich in oil.

similar_questions.stem: Legume crops grown for their protein-rich seeds are
explanation_steps: Pulses = grain legumes.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following crops are grown to improve the fertility of the soil?
explanation_steps: Textbook: green manure crops are ploughed in while green, before they produce seed, 'so that they can provide nitrogen to the soil' (clover, alfalfa, soybean, vetch, cowpea).
Cover crops mainly protect the soil from erosion. Answer: E.
tips: Green manure → fertility; cover crop → erosion control; trap crop → pest control.

similar_questions.stem: Crops grown mainly to protect the soil surface from erosion are
explanation_steps: Cover crops cover and protect the soil.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: All of the following are reasons of decline in wildlife except,
explanation_steps: Habitat destruction, drought, illegal trade and over-hunting reduce wildlife numbers.
Sustainable (controlled) wildlife trade is a conservation-compatible use, not a cause of decline. Answer: E.
tips: 'Sustainable' use means harvesting no more than the population can replace.

similar_questions.stem: Which measure helps to conserve wildlife?
explanation_steps: Protected areas conserve habitats.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is derived from the remains of food processing industries or slaughter houses to be used in improving the fertility of soils?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Organic fertilizers are waste products derived from the processing industries or slaughterhouses and compost used as organic fertilizers.'
Urea, TSP, DAP and ammonium nitrate are manufactured inorganic fertilizers; compost is the only organic fertilizer offered. Answer: E.
tips: Organic N sources: oil-seed cakes, blood, horn and hoof meal, manure, compost.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is an inorganic fertilizer?
explanation_steps: Urea is a manufactured nitrogen fertilizer (46 % N).
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Repetitive growing of the same crop grown alone in pure stand in a piece of land is termed as
explanation_steps: Mono-cropping: one crop grown alone (pure stand), often repeatedly on the same land.
Mixed/intercropping grow two or more crops together; relay cropping sows the second crop before the first is harvested. Answer: B.
tips: Crop rotation is the remedy for the problems of continuous mono-cropping.

similar_questions.stem: Growing two or more crops simultaneously in distinct rows on the same field is
explanation_steps: Crops together in rows = (row) intercropping.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following groups of crops are classified based on their life span.

options.A: Vegetables, fruit crops and cereal crops
options.B: Field crops, horticultural crops and cereals
options.C: Oil crops, pulse crops and cereal crops
options.D: Annual crops, biennial crops and perennial crops

explanation_steps: By life span, crops are annual (one season), biennial (two seasons) or perennial (many years).
The other groups classify by use or by type of production. Answer: D.
tips: Onion and cabbage (for seed) are biennials; coffee, citrus and banana are perennials.

similar_questions.stem: A crop that completes its life cycle in two growing seasons is
explanation_steps: Two seasons = biennial.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Transplanting involves

options.A: the use of plastic netting for shading.
options.B: the removal of excess plants so that the remaining plants could get enough space.
options.C: sowing in seed beds or seed trays.
options.D: transfer of seedlings from the seed beds, seed trays to containers and a nursery field.

explanation_steps: Transplanting is moving seedlings from seed beds or seed trays into containers or the field.
B is thinning, A is shading and C is sowing. Answer: D.
tips: Nursery practices: shading, watering, thinning, pricking-out/transplanting, pruning, hardening-off, grading.

similar_questions.stem: Removing some seedlings so that the remaining ones get enough space and nutrients is called
explanation_steps: Textbook definition of thinning.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.5.3 Nursery Establishment and Management – nursery practices

questions.stem: Which of the following practices is the cheapest and safest method of pest control?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The use of insect-resistant varieties is the cheapest and best method of insect control in crop plants.'
Answer: C.
tips: Chemical control is the last resort (cost, residues, resistance, environment).

similar_questions.stem: Why is chemical control recommended as the last resort?

options.B: It can harm the environment and leave residues

explanation_steps: Pesticides pollute and leave residues; pests develop resistance.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases – insect control

questions.stem: All of the following are systems of surface irrigation except
explanation_steps: Surface irrigation lets water flow over the soil surface by gravity: flood, furrow, basin, border and spate (flood diversion) irrigation.
Sprinkler irrigation sprays water under pressure – it is an overhead (pressurised) system. Answer: C.
tips: Pressurised systems: sprinkler and drip (trickle).

similar_questions.stem: Which irrigation method delivers water drop by drop near the root zone?
explanation_steps: Drip (trickle) irrigation.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a water harvesting technique?

options.C: Construction of reservoirs or ponds along rivers

explanation_steps: The textbook's water-harvesting section (3.4) covers dams, ponds, river diversion, wells, and roof and rock-outcrop water harvesting.
All of A–D are therefore water-harvesting techniques. Answer: E.
tips: When every option is listed in the textbook, choose 'None of the above' in a 'not' question.

similar_questions.stem: Collecting rainwater from a corrugated iron roof into a tank is
explanation_steps: Textbook 3.4.5 roof and rock-outcrop water harvesting.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is not true about irrigation systems.

options.A: Surface irrigation is a traditional system.
options.B: Sprinkler irrigation is a modern system compared to drip irrigation.
options.C: Flood irrigation has historically been the most common method of irrigation.
options.D: Sprinkler and drip irrigation systems are cheaper to establish and maintain than surface irrigation systems.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about calves?

questions.stem: How do weeds affect the growth and production of the main crop? (1.5 points)
questions.answer: Weeds compete with the crop for nutrients, moisture (water), light and space, so the crop grows poorly and yields fall. They also host insect pests and diseases, reduce the quality of the produce (weed seeds mixed with grain), make field operations and harvesting harder, and some are poisonous or cause health problems.
explanation_steps: Textbook harmful effects of weeds: competition for nutrients, moisture, light and space → reduced growth and yield loss.
Weeds harbour pests and diseases, lower the quality of produce, raise production costs and can reduce land value.
For 1.5 points give three effects (0.5 each), starting with competition.
marking_points: 0.5 each for any three: competition for nutrients / water / light / space (each competition factor may count once or grouped as one); host pests and diseases; reduce quality of produce; increase cost of production / interfere with operations; poisonous/health hazards; reduce land value.
tips: Remember 'N-M-L-S': Nutrients, Moisture, Light, Space.

similar_questions.stem: Give two ways in which weeds can be useful to a farmer.
similar_questions.answer: Any two: animal feed; compost/manure; medicine; construction material; soil cover that reduces erosion.
explanation_steps: The textbook lists these benefits alongside the harmful effects.

questions.stem:
Write a short note on the following terms. (4.5 points)
2.1 Deforestation
2.2 Afforestation
2.3 Reforestation
questions.answer:
2.1 Deforestation: the removal or clearing of existing forest cover (mainly by human activities – clearing for farmland, fuel wood, overgrazing, settlement), so that the land is converted to non-forest use.
2.2 Afforestation: establishing a forest by planting (or seeding) trees on land that has not been forested for a long time (e.g. about 20 years or more) or has never carried forest.
2.3 Reforestation: re-establishing a forest on land from which forest was recently removed (by cutting, fire etc.), by replanting or natural regeneration.

subparts.question: Deforestation
subparts.answer: Removal/clearing of existing forest cover, mainly by human activity, converting it to non-forest use.
steps: Causes: farmland expansion, fuel wood, overgrazing, settlement.

subparts.question: Afforestation
subparts.answer: Establishing forest by planting trees on land not forested for a long time (≈ 20 years) or never forested.

subparts.question: Reforestation
subparts.answer: Re-establishing forest on land where forest was recently cut or destroyed.

explanation_steps: Deforestation = loss of forest (human-induced removal of forest cover).
Afforestation = new forest where none existed recently/ever.
Reforestation = replacing forest that was recently removed.
1.5 points for each correct note.
marking_points: 2.1 (1.5): removal/clearing of forest cover (by human activity) and conversion to other land use.
2.2 (1.5): planting trees/creating forest on land that was not forested (recently or ever).
2.3 (1.5): re-establishing forest on land where forest was recently removed.
tips: Af- = 'add a new forest'; Re- = 'again'; De- = 'remove'.

similar_questions.stem: Planting eucalyptus on a hillside that has been bare grazing land for 50 years is an example of which practice?
similar_questions.answer: Afforestation – the land has not carried forest for a long time.
explanation_steps: Afforestation applies to land not forested for ≥ about 20 years or never forested.

questions.stem:
List down any four methods of pest control that could be applied in field crops to improve productivity. (4 points)
3.1 ______
3.2 ______
3.3 ______

questions.answer: Any four of: (1) mechanical/physical control (hand-picking, trapping, destroying infested plants); (2) cultural/crop-management practices (crop rotation, timely planting, field sanitation, deep ploughing); (3) biological control (natural enemies – predators, parasites); (4) chemical control (pesticides/insecticides); (5) use of resistant varieties; (6) integrated pest management (IPM) combining these.
explanation_steps: The textbook describes insect/pest control by mechanical methods, crop-management practices, biological control, chemical control and resistant varieties.
1 point per correctly named method (with a short example if possible).
marking_points: 1 point each for any four: mechanical/physical; cultural (crop management); biological; chemical; resistant varieties; IPM.
tips: Remember 'M-C-B-C-R': Mechanical, Cultural, Biological, Chemical, Resistant varieties.

questions.stem: What is the objective of quarantine in the prevention of common diseases in livestock? (2 points)
questions.answer: Quarantine is the separation of seemingly healthy animals that have been exposed to the risk of infection (e.g. newly bought or imported animals) from the healthy herd for a period based on the incubation period of the disease. Its objective is to find out whether these animals harbour infection or not, and so prevent the introduction and spread of contagious diseases to healthy animals, farms or the country.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p75): 'Quarantine – this is the separation of seemingly healthy animals that have been exposed to the risk of infection from healthy animals. The objective of this is to ascertain whether these animals harbour infection or not.' The period depends on the incubation period of the disease.
Glossary: quarantine – measures to prevent the import/export of unwanted organisms.
In livestock health: newly introduced or sick animals are kept separately (isolated) and observed; movement of animals is restricted during outbreaks.
Two points: isolation of new/sick animals (1) + to prevent introduction/spread of disease (1).
marking_points: 1 point: separating (isolating) exposed / newly introduced animals from the healthy herd for a set period.
1 point: to ascertain whether they harbour infection, and so prevent introduction/spread of disease to healthy animals.
tips: Quarantine = isolate + observe → stop spread.

similar_questions.stem: Name two other ways, besides quarantine, of preventing livestock diseases.
similar_questions.answer: Any two: vaccination; good hygiene/sanitation of houses; control of vectors (dipping/spraying for ticks); proper feeding; deworming; culling sick animals.
explanation_steps: Textbook disease-prevention measures.

questions.stem:
Give any three advantages of beekeeping over other types of livestock production. (3 points)
5.1 ______
5.2 ______
5.3 ______
questions.answer: Any three: (1) it needs little capital (low start-up and running costs); (2) it needs very little land, and the land need not be fertile; (3) it can be done by men and women of any age; (4) it can be a part-time/secondary activity alongside other work; (5) bees do not need feeding or grazing land and do not compete with crops; (6) bees pollinate crops, raising yields; (7) products (honey, wax) are valuable and store well.
explanation_steps: Textbook: beekeeping requires low capital, little land of any quality, is suitable for both sexes and all ages, and can be done as a secondary activity; bees also pollinate crops.
1 point per advantage.
marking_points: 1 point each for any three valid advantages (low capital; little land/any land; both sexes and all ages; secondary activity; pollination; no feed required; valuable products).
tips: Think about what bees do NOT need compared with cattle: feed, water, big land, big capital.

similar_questions.stem: Name two products of beekeeping.
similar_questions.answer: Honey and beeswax (also propolis, pollen, royal jelly).
explanation_steps: Main products: honey and wax.

questions.stem: Explain reasons as to why soil and water conservation is important for Eritrea. (5 points)
questions.answer: Eritrea lies in the Sudano-Sahelian zone with low, erratic and intense rainfall, and much of it has steep slopes. Centuries of deforestation, overgrazing and cultivation of slopes have left the land (especially the highlands) severely degraded. Soil is lost 20–40 times faster than it forms; soil loss reduces soil depth, fertility and water-holding capacity, and yields have fallen by 30–90 % in places (productivity about halved). Most people depend on rain-fed agriculture, so conserving soil and water is necessary to: keep fertile topsoil in place; increase infiltration and soil moisture for crops; recharge groundwater, wells and springs; reduce runoff, flooding and siltation of dams; restore vegetation; and so achieve food security and sustainable development.
explanation_steps: Climate: arid/semi-arid, low and erratic rainfall – every drop must be conserved.
Land degradation: deforestation, overgrazing, cultivation of steep slopes; erosion 20–40 × faster than soil formation.
Effects: loss of fertile topsoil and nutrients, decline in yields (30–90 %), siltation of reservoirs, drying of springs.
Benefits of SWC: more soil moisture, groundwater recharge, higher and stable yields, rehabilitation of degraded land, food security for a mostly rural population.
Award about 1 point per well-explained reason (five reasons).
marking_points: About 1 point each for five explained reasons: low/erratic rainfall (water scarcity); severe erosion/land degradation (loss rate ≫ formation); loss of soil fertility and yields; groundwater recharge/water supply; reduce runoff/flooding/siltation; food security & livelihoods of rain-fed farmers; rehabilitation of vegetation/environment.
tips: Structure: problem (climate + degradation) → consequence (lower yields, water shortage) → benefit of SWC.

similar_questions.stem: Give two physical (structural) soil and water conservation measures used in Eritrea.
similar_questions.answer: Any two: terraces (bench/stone terraces), stone bunds / soil bunds, check dams, hillside terraces, micro-basins, trenches.
explanation_steps: Textbook SWC measures.
